appearance: Large eye and relatively deep body
biology: Spend most of life in saltwater and reproduce in freshwater
Reproduction in the Hudson River occurs from late March to early May
diet: Fish eggs and larval fish
Insects
Zooplankton
ecosystem: Component of the forage base for coastal fishes, marine mammals and seabirds, but also terrestrial animals and shorebirds
monitoring: Ecologically and economically important species
Population changes can reveal broader ecosystem level changes
fact: It is thought that a fish will return to reproduce in the same river in which they were born

image.credit: Photo: Connecticut Department of Energy & Environmental Protection

appearance: Thin metallic body varying in color from greenish to dark blue
Large dark shoulder spot may be followed by several paler spots
biology: Reproduction in the Hudson River occurs on sandy, gravelly shoals and other shallow areas
A female may release 100,000 to 600,000 eggs
diet: Juveniles eat zooplankton and terrestrial insects
Feed on plankton, crustaceans, and small fish in the ocean
ecosystem: Migratory link between the river and open ocean – transporting nutrients between the systems
Food source to larger fish, birds, and some terrestrial animals
monitoring: Historically very abundant and now population reduced to low levels – important to track population recovery
fact: The Shadbush tree is named after this fish because the spring bloom aligns with the return of shad for river reproduction

image.credit: Photo: Virginia Institute of Marine Science

appearance: Have a series of bony plates called scutes on their back, sides, and belly
biology: Adults return to the Hudson River to spawn in May and June
Young fish remain in their natal river for up to 6 years before swimming out to the ocean
diet: Bottom-feeders that primarily eat crustaceans, mollusks, insects, and worms
ecosystem: Regulate benthic prey populations
monitoring: Listed under the Endangered Species Act and population recovery is a key goal
fact: This is the largest sturgeon species found in New York

appearance: Reach up to 9-12 inches in length
Three distinct dorsal fins and two anal fins
biology: Rarely live past 1 year old in the Hudson River
Primarily demersal and reproduce from November to February over gravel and sand
diet: Juveniles eat copepods and small amphipods
Adults eat small crustaceans, shellfish, worms, and other fish
ecosystem: Important prey for larger predatory fish
monitoring: Can be used for tracing chemical contaminants as they tend to accumulate high concentrations in polluted areas
fact: Have developed the ability to produce antifreeze proteins making them very tolerant of cold water temperatures

image.credit: Photo: Connecticut Department of Energy & Environmental Protection

appearance: Slender and grows up to 4 inches in length
Silvery-green with a translucent body and a silver stripe on its sides
biology: Schooling fish
Can reach maturity at around 2.5 months
Reproduce in the nighttime between April and September
diet: Fish less than 25 mm eat planktonic copepods and larvae
Larger fish eat amphipods, ostracods, and small mollusks
ecosystem: Important forage fish for many other birds and recreationally and commercially important fishes
monitoring: Good indicator of estuary pollution stress
fact: Adults may live to be slightly older than 3 years old, but few often survive past their first year

image.credit: Photo: Virginia Institute of Marine Science

appearance: Bluish green top coloration and overall silvery color
Usually have a dark spot located just behind the gill plate on the upper side of the body
biology: Schooling species
Reproduce in the Hudson River during late spring and early summer
diet: Planktivore – consumes copepods, pelagic shrimp larvae and larval fishes
ecosystem: Important food web link – eat plankton and they themselves are then eaten by larger predatory fish and birds
monitoring: Important forage base for larger predators
fact: Blueback herring and alewife are collectively termed “river herring”

image.credit: Photo: Connecticut Department of Energy & Environmental Protection

appearance: Steel to greenish blue color on upper parts, fading to silver on lower sides and belly
Forked tail and streamlined body with sharp teeth
biology: Live up to 12 years
Reproduce multiple times in the spring and summer
Females can produce over 400,000 eggs or more
diet: Fish, including bay anchovy and silversides
Invertebrates
ecosystem: Voracious apex predator fish regulating smaller forage fish populations
monitoring: Assess population status
Track PCB contamination levels
fact: Baby bluefish are known as snappers

image.credit: Photo: Virginia Institute of Marine Science

appearance: Bluish or greenish gray body with a silvery white belly and olive fins
Four pairs of barbels around mouth
biology: Parents build nests like under rocks or in submerged hollow logs and guard young
Life span varies greatly but some may live for over 25 years
diet: Bottom feeders eating aquatic insects, arthropods, and fish
ecosystem: Invasive species that could outcompete native catfish species like the white catfish
monitoring: Non-native invasive species impacts
fact: Have taste receptors all over their body, with the highest concentration located on the four pairs of barbels (“whiskers”)

appearance: Small head and mouth with a short and blunt snout
biology: Reproduce near the surface during mid to late spring
Occur mainly in freshwater but can be found in brackish or saline waters
diet: Newly hatched larvae eat protozoans and other plankton
Diet later includes detritus, algae, and phytoplankton
ecosystem: Forage fish for valued game fishes
monitoring: Tracking population changes can reveal information about broader ecosystem changes
fact: Named for its unique muscular stomach that functions like a bird’s gizzard – use ingested sand or small stones to grind up food

image.credit: Photo: Connecticut Department of Energy & Environmental Protection

appearance: Brownish-gray body with vertical lines and spots
biology: Bottom-dweller preferring sand, silt, or mud
Peak reproduction in July and early-August
Can live up to 7 years old
diet: Worms
Amphipods and other small crustaceans
Small fish
ecosystem: Important predators in benthic food web
monitoring: Close connection to the bottom can indicate water quality and habitat health
fact: It is said that when farmers would feed the fish to pigs, they would choke on them due to the rough scales, hence their name

image.credit: Photo: Connecticut Department of Energy & Environmental Protection

biology: Reproduce in the spring in freshwater at night
Can produce an antifreeze protein to enable survival at subfreezing temperatures
diet: Aquatic insects, worms, small crustaceans, fish
ecosystem: Prey for larger predatory fish and birds
monitoring: Broader ecosystem level changes can be revealed by tracking population changes
fact: When this fish is taken out of the water, it gives off the odor of freshly cut cucumbers

image.credit: Photo: New Hampshire Fish & Game Department

appearance: Short conical snout with 4 barbels in front of the mouth
Five rows of scutes: one on the back, two on the belly, and one on each side
biology: Reproduction is associated with gravel-dominated bottom-types
Reproduction in the Hudson River occurs from April to May
diet: Worms, insect larvae, plants, snails, shrimp, crayfish
ecosystem: Benthic scavenger regulating invertebrate populations
monitoring: Listed under the Endangered Species Act
Maintain recovery of the population in the Hudson River
fact: The oldest female ever recorded was 67 years old and the oldest male was 32 years old

appearance: Distinct black spot at base of tail
biology: Small, schooling fish found in freshwater and brackish habitats
Spawn during warmer months (June-July)
diet: Omnivores. Eat small aquatic organisms including insect larvae, crustaceans, and zooplankton
ecosystem: Forage fish in the Hudson River food web
Key food source for larger predatory fish and wading birds
monitoring: Important forage fish species
Tracking changes in the population over time helps reveal broader changes in the Hudson River ecosystem
fact: The Spottail Shiner was named after the Hudson River!
Their scientific name, hudsonius, means “of the Hudson.”

image.credit: Photo: Robert Aguilar/Smithsonian Environmental Research Center, CC BY 2.0

biology: Bottom dwelling; found in shallow, slow-moving waters
Uses large pectoral fins to help rest and move on bottom
Spawn in spring
diet: Small crustaceans
Insects and insect larvae
Snails
Algae
ecosystem: Serve as food source for larger fish and birds
Help to regulate invertebrate populations
monitoring: Their close connection to bottom habitats can help indicate local water quality and habitat health
fact: Darters get their name from the way they quickly “dart” along the river bottom!

biology: Bottom dwelling freshwater fish
Most active evening through nighttime
Builds nests; guards young
diet: Opportunistic feeder
Aquatic insects, crustaceans, small fish, mollusks
ecosystem: Adult fish are important predators
Young white catfish are an important prey species for larger predatory fish such as the Striped Bass
monitoring: As bottom dwellers, they reflect local water and habitat quality.
Can accumulate pollutants like heavy metals, helping inform safe fish consumption advisories
fact: White Catfish can live for more than a decade!

image.credit: Illustration: Duane Raver/U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service

appearance: Deep, laterally compressed body. Can grow up to 22 inches. Silvery-white, with two dorsal fins slightly joined by a membrane.
biology: Semi-anadromous
R-selected species
Reaches maturity at ~ 2-4 years
diet: Ranges from fish eggs, invertebrates, to small fish like minnows
ecosystem: Prolific mid-trophic level species linking lower and higher trophic level species
monitoring: Helps inform ecosystem–based management
fact: In the Hudson River, there are both resident and migratory populations

editorial_repairs.original: In the Hudson River, can be up to 5-6ft in length
Reproduce in rivers every 2-5 years during the spring
editorial_repairs.display: Adults return to the Hudson River to spawn in May and June

editorial_repairs.original: Deep and laterally compressed body. Can grow up to 22 inch Silvery-white with two dorsal fins slightly joined by a membrane
editorial_repairs.display: Deep, laterally compressed body. Can grow up to 22 inches. Silvery-white, with two dorsal fins slightly joined by a membrane.
